opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot as a kind of speciation. Right now the labs are going for one giant oracle that knows everything and does everything, and that makes sense as a starting point because you get a lot of transfer. Training on code makes it better at reasoning, training on math helps elsewhere, so there's a real argument for one big blob.

But if you look at biology, or really any complex system, you don't end up with one organism that does everything. You get a whole ecosystem, with niches and specialization. I think we'll see something similar. A huge model is overkill for a lot of tasks. If you're running something billions of times a day, or on a device, or with tight latency, you don't want to pay for a trillion parameters that remember obscure facts about medieval history when you just need it to be really good at one thing.

There's also this idea I keep coming back to, a "cognitive core." You could strip a model down so it has the algorithms for thinking, reasoning, and tool use, but doesn't have to memorize the whole internet, because it can look things up. That core could be pretty small. Then you specialize it: fine-tune it, give it the right context and tools for a domain, and it becomes very capable and very cheap in that niche.

So I don't think it's either-or. The big general models will keep pushing the frontier and act as teachers. You'll distill from them and spin off lots of smaller specialized models that fill different niches. The tooling for that isn't great yet, and fine-tuning without losing capabilities is still a bit of an art, but I expect it to get much easier. Then you'll see a lot more diversity in the model population, and less of a single monoculture.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI specialization to biological ecosystems and niche specialization, but does not clearly mention diversity in animal brains adapted to different ecological niches.

r002.rationale: It describes a smaller cognitive core that retains reasoning and tool-use abilities, then can be specialized for a domain.

r003.rationale: It says specialized models can be much cheaper for their target niche and motivates them by device and latency constraints, communicating improved inference efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a very strong pull from the labs toward a single model that does everything, because that's what scaling has been rewarding. You throw more compute and more data at one big network and it gets better across the board, and so the natural thing to do is keep doing that. But I don't think that pull is the whole story, and there are a few reasons I expect a lot of specialized models to show up alongside it.

The first one is just economics. A frontier model is incredibly expensive to run, and most of what people actually want to do with AI is fairly narrow. If you're classifying support tickets, or generating SQL against your own schema, or doing some specific kind of document extraction, you do not need a model that also knows Shakespeare and can write a compiler. You need something that does your thing extremely well, cheaply, and fast. And it turns out that if you take a small model and you train it hard on a narrow distribution, often with data generated by the big model, you can get something that matches or beats the frontier on that one task at a tiny fraction of the cost. That's just too good a deal for people not to take.

The second reason is that a lot of the value is going to be in the data, and the data is not evenly distributed. The big labs can scrape the internet, but they can't scrape the inside of a hospital system, or a specific company's codebase and incident history, or a chip design flow. Whoever has that data has an edge, and the way you exploit that edge is you build or fine-tune a model around it. That's inherently a specialization story. The general model becomes more like a foundation, and then there's this whole layer of things built on top of it that know things the foundation doesn't.

The third reason is kind of a historical analogy I keep coming back to. If you look at computing, we did not end up with one CPU that does everything. We ended up with CPUs, but also GPUs, and then TPUs, and DSPs, and all these accelerators, because once you understand a workload well enough, you can build something much more efficient for it. I think the same thing happens with neural networks. The general model is the CPU. It's flexible, it runs everything, it's what you reach for when you don't know what you're doing yet. But once a workload becomes stable and important, people will carve it out into something specialized.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that I don't think the general model and the specialized models are really in competition. The general model is often the thing that makes the specialized ones possible. It's the teacher, it generates the synthetic data, it does the hard reasoning once so you can distill it down. So I see it less as a fork in the road and more as a stack. You have a small number of very large generalists at the top, and then a long tail of smaller, cheaper, faster models underneath that are tuned to the shape of the actual work. I think both of those get built, and I think both of them matter.

r001.rationale: The response compares specialized models to computing hardware such as CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs, but does not mention animal brains or ecological niches.

r002.rationale: It says a small model trained on a narrow distribution can match or beat a frontier model on that task, communicating task competence at a smaller model size.

r003.rationale: It says specialized models can perform narrow tasks extremely well, cheaply, and fast, and describes them as smaller and more efficient for stable workloads.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two forces here. There’s a strong incentive to consolidate everything into one model because knowledge transfers across domains. Learning to code can help you reason, and so on. So having a very capable general model makes a lot of sense.

But if you have a particular application, you don’t necessarily want to pay for all of that capability on every single query. You care about how good the model is at your task, how fast it is, and how much it costs. And you may have a very specific distribution of problems, with data and feedback that let you optimize for that distribution.

So I expect the big models to be general-purpose systems, but also to help create smaller, specialized models—by generating training data, for example. If you know exactly what job you need done, you can potentially distill that capability into something much cheaper and faster. Those seem like complementary things to me.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two forces here. On one hand, the labs want to build a single model that can do everything, and there are real benefits to that because knowledge transfers across domains. Learning to code might actually help you reason about something else.

But at deployment time, you have a specific task, a latency requirement, and a budget. If you’re doing the same relatively narrow task millions of times, you probably don’t want to pay for this enormous model that also knows how to write poetry and speak twenty languages. You want something smaller that does your particular thing really well.

So I expect an ecosystem where the big general models help train or distill these specialized models. The general model is sort of the teacher, and you can produce a much cheaper, faster model for a particular application. Those seem very complementary to me. You can have increasingly capable general intelligence at the frontier and, simultaneously, a huge proliferation of specialized models that actually do a lot of the work.
